sections.title: Verbs followed by a wh-clause
sections.content:
Some verbs can be followed by a clause beginning with a wh-word (how, what, when, where, which, who, or why):
• That might explain why he's unhappy.
• I couldn't decide which train to catch.
Also: arrange, calculate, check, choose, debate, determine, discover, discuss, establish, find out, forget, guess, imagine, know, learn, notice, plan, realise, remember, say, see, talk about, think (about), understand, wonder.
Many of these can also be followed by a wh-clause (except 'why') + to-infinitive:
• Did you find out where to go? (but not ... find out why to go)

sections.title: Verbs requiring an object before the wh-clause
sections.content:
Some verbs must have an object before the wh-clause:
• She reminded me what (I had) to do.
• I told Linda how to get to my house.
Also: advise, inform, instruct, teach, warn. Ask and show often have an object, but not always.

sections.title: Whether vs If and That
sections.content:
We can use whether in a wh-clause to show choices. It has a similar meaning to 'if'. However, 'if' is never used before a to-infinitive:
• You have 14 days to decide whether to keep it or not. (not ... decide if to keep it ...)
Note the difference between whether and that:
• I didn't know whether the shop was shut. (= if it was shut or not)
• I didn't know that the shop was shut. (suggests it was definitely shut)

exercises.question: Before the meeting finished they arranged ___ to meet next.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: when
After 'arrange', you can use a wh-word + to-infinitive: 'arranged when to meet', 'arranged where to go'. This is a verb + wh-clause + infinitive construction.

exercises.sentence: Could you tell me what time does the last train leave?
exercises.correction: Could you tell me what time the last train leaves?
acceptable: what time the last train leaves
exercises.hint: In indirect questions, use statement word order (subject + verb), not question inversion.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: what time the last train leaves
After reporting/question verbs followed by 'wh-' words (tell me, ask, wonder, know, understand), use statement word order: 'what time the train leaves' (NOT 'leaves the train'). The auxiliary 'does' disappears in indirect speech: 'does leave' → 'leaves'.

exercises.question: He took my hands and showed ___ to fit the parts back together.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: me how
Show + object + how + to-infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.sentence: I wonder that she will accept the offer.
exercises.correction: I wonder whether she will accept the offer.
acceptable: I wonder if she will accept the offer
I wonder whether she will accept the offer
exercises.hint: 'Wonder' is followed by 'if' or 'whether', not 'that', for yes/no questions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I wonder whether/if she will accept
'Wonder' followed by 'that' expresses surprise ('I wonder that she accepted'). For indirect yes/no questions, use 'wonder if/whether': 'I wonder if she will accept' = I am not sure whether she will accept. This meaning requires 'if' or 'whether', not 'that'.

exercises.question: She was ___ whether to invite Jeremy over for dinner.
exercises.hint: Debate/consider/choose can be followed by whether + to-infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: debating
Debate/consider/choose can be followed by whether + to-infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.sentence: No one could explain how did the accident happen.
exercises.correction: No one could explain how the accident happened.
exercises.hint: After 'explain', use statement word order — not question inversion with 'did'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: how the accident happened
After verbs like 'explain', 'understand', 'know', 'describe', 'show', indirect questions always use statement word order (subject + verb). 'How did the accident happen?' is a direct question. As an indirect question (after 'explain'), it becomes 'how the accident happened' — no 'did', normal word order.

exercises.question: The council is meeting to ___ whether to increase local taxes.
exercises.hint: Discuss fits the context of a meeting better.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: discuss
Discuss fits the context of a meeting better.

exercises.question: I couldn't decide ___ to carry on or go back down.
exercises.hint: Only 'whether' is used before a to-infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: whether
Only 'whether' is used before a to-infinitive. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: Fortunately, my years in the Andes had taught ___ what to do in extreme conditions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: me
'Teach' requires both an indirect object (the person taught) and a direct object: 'teach someone something' or 'teach someone to do something'. Without the person, the sentence is incomplete.
